R05-C-01: An economy organised entirely by prices would have no need of firms. Every task, from sweeping a floor to designing a circuit, could be bought from whoever offered it most cheaply, and each worker would be a small business selling services by the hour. That actual economies look nothing like this is so familiar that it rarely seems to require explanation. Yet it does. Inside a firm, resources move not because a price has changed but because someone has been told to move them, and the coexistence of these two methods of coordination, the market outside and the hierarchy within, is one of the quieter puzzles of economic life. The standard answer is that using the market is not free. Before anything can be bought, a buyer must find sellers, compare their terms, write a contract and then check that the contract has been honoured. When a task recurs daily and its details cannot be specified in advance, these costs multiply, and it becomes cheaper to hire someone on open-ended terms and direct the work as it arises. On this view the firm is a device for economising on bargaining: it grows until the cost of organising one more activity internally equals the cost of buying it outside. The account has real explanatory power. It predicts, correctly, that firms tend to bring in-house the activities that are specific to their own operations, where a supplier who knew it was indispensable could hold them to ransom. What the account leaves out is suggested by its own vocabulary. It describes the firm almost entirely in terms of costs avoided, as if the best a firm could do were to match what an ideal market would have delivered at no expense. But a group of people who work together for years does not merely save on contracts; it produces something that no contract could have bought. Such a group learns which of its members can be trusted with ambiguity, how to divide a problem that none of them fully understands, and which shortcuts are safe. This knowledge is rarely written down and often cannot be, because it lives in habits and in the expectations people hold of one another. It cannot be purchased from outside because it does not exist outside; it is a product of the firm's continued existence. None of this overturns the bargaining view, which remains the best guide to where the boundary of a firm will fall in any particular case. A carmaker deciding whether to make its own seats is weighing exactly the costs that view describes. The difficulty arises only when the account is taken as a complete theory of what firms are for. Then it makes the firm look like a regrettable necessity, a patch over the imperfections of exchange, and it renders the most valuable thing a firm possesses, the shared competence of people who have learned to work together, invisible to the very analysis that claims to explain it.
R05-C-02: A piece of folk wisdom, repeated in many places, holds that a family business rarely survives the founder's grandchildren. The founder builds it through hard work, the children keep it going out of duty, and the grandchildren, raised in comfort, let it slip away. The story is usually told as a lesson about character: wealth softens those who inherit it, and the hunger that built the firm cannot be handed down along with the shares. It is a satisfying story, and like most satisfying stories it is only partly true. Consider first the plain arithmetic of inheritance. A founder typically owns the whole firm and answers to no one. If the shares are divided among three children, and each of them divides theirs among three more, the third generation may consist of nine or more owners, some of whom work in the business and some of whom have never set foot in it. Those who draw a salary want the profits reinvested; those who live elsewhere want dividends; those who need cash want to sell, and there may be no agreed price at which the others can buy them out. Quarrels follow, but they follow from the structure, and the most energetic cousin in the world could not make them disappear. A second difficulty lies in how leaders are chosen. A firm that insists the chief executive must be a member of the family has narrowed its field of candidates to a handful of people who happen to share a surname. Even if every one of them is capable, the chance that the best available manager is among them is small. The founder often makes matters worse by postponing the question altogether, because the business is so bound up with his sense of who he is that planning for his own departure feels like planning for his death. When the moment can no longer be avoided, it tends to arrive suddenly, through illness or a quarrel, and the successor is whoever is standing nearest. None of this means that character is irrelevant; some heirs are indeed less driven than their parents, and some fortunes really are spent rather than lost. But the family firms that last for many generations tend to have one thing in common, and it is not a lucky supply of hard-working grandchildren. They separate the role of owner from the role of manager, write down rules for how shares may be sold within the family, and are willing to hire an outsider to run the business when no relative is suited to it. Their survival is less a triumph of virtue than of design.
R05-C-03: When a dominant company is overtaken by a newcomer, the explanation usually offered is some version of complacency: its managers, the story goes, grew comfortable, stopped listening to the market and failed to perceive what was approaching. The story has the appeal of a fable, and it permits the rest of us to believe that an identical fate could be avoided simply by remaining vigilant. Its difficulty is that, in many of the best known cases, the incumbent's managers were neither lazy nor blind. They were doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do. The pattern runs roughly as follows. A new technology appears that is, at first, worse than the existing one by the measures that the incumbent's best customers care about. It is slower, or less precise, or less durable, but it is cheaper and simpler, and it finds a small market among buyers who were never well served by the established product. The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no. It examines the margins, and they are thin. It looks at the size of the market, and it is too small to move a company of its scale. Every one of these judgements is correct, and together they lead the firm to put its money where its profits are. Meanwhile the new technology improves, year by year, until it is good enough for the mainstream, and the incumbent discovers that its careful attention to its best customers has left it with nothing to offer the rest. It may be objected that this account is written with the convenient clarity of hindsight, since for every cheap technology that grew up to displace its betters, many others remained toys and disappeared, and an incumbent that chased all of them would have squandered its resources. The objection is fair, but it strengthens rather than weakens the point. If good managers cannot tell in advance which small markets will matter, then vigilance alone cannot be the remedy, because the problem is not a failure to look but a set of rules for deciding what is worth looking at. What seems to help is therefore structural rather than psychological: firms that have survived such transitions have often placed the new venture in a separate unit, with its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it. This is no guarantee, since separate units can be starved or smothered by the parent organisation, but the arrangement at least removes the new business from the scrutiny of the rules that would have judged it, correctly by their own lights, not worth the trouble.
R05-C-04: Business journalism has a favourite kind of hero: the chief executive who arrives at a struggling company, takes bold decisions and turns it around. Magazine profiles, admiring biographies and conference speeches all tell the story in the same way, with the leader at the centre and everything else as scenery. The habit is understandable, since a firm is an abstraction and it is far easier to praise or blame a person than a set of market conditions. But the habit also produces a systematic error about how much any one leader actually controls. Consider what else moves a company's results. Demand for its products rises and falls with the economy and with the fortunes of its industry; the price of its raw materials is set in markets it cannot influence; many of the products it sells were conceived years earlier, under managers who have since left. A new chief executive who takes over at the bottom of a downturn will, in the ordinary course of things, preside over a recovery, and the recovery will be credited to him. His successor, arriving at the peak, will be blamed for the decline that follows. Neither may have done much to cause what happened while he was in charge. Imagine two firms in the same industry, with similar products and similar costs. One appoints a celebrated leader just as the market begins to recover; the other keeps an unremarkable manager who has run it for years. Both firms prosper over the next three years, but only one of them is written about, and the story of its revival will attribute to leadership what was largely a rising market carrying both firms upward. Such comparisons are rarely made, because the second firm has no story to tell. None of this means that leaders are irrelevant. In moments of genuine crisis, or when a firm must choose between strategies that will shape it for decades, the judgement of the person at the top can matter a great deal. The error lies in degree, not in kind. Yet the error has consequences, for boards that believe in saviours go looking for them outside the firm, pay them accordingly, and dismiss them when results return to the ordinary, only to begin the search again. An organisation that understood how much of its fate lay beyond any individual might spend less on heroes and more on the people and systems that carry it through every leader's tenure.
R05-C-05: Few management practices divide opinion as sharply as forced ranking, the system in which managers must place a fixed share of their staff in each band of a performance scale, so that some employees are always rated outstanding, most are rated adequate and a few are always rated poor, often with the expectation that the last group will leave. Its defenders make a reasonable case. Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all. A forced distribution, on this view, simply obliges managers to say what they already know. The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to. It assumes, first, that performance within each team is spread along a curve, so that any group of a dozen people must contain its stars and its laggards. In a large population this may be roughly true, but a small team may have been assembled precisely because all its members are good, and forcing a distribution upon it manufactures distinctions that the work itself does not support. It assumes, second, that performance belongs to individuals, when in most organisations the results that matter are produced by people working together, and the contribution of any one of them is hard to separate from that of the rest. The second assumption matters most, because of what the system teaches. If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me, and sharing an idea is a gift to a rival. The employees who learn this lesson fastest are not necessarily the most capable; they are the most attentive to how they appear. Over time, able people may also learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues than among excellent ones. A system introduced to reward merit ends by rewarding position. It would be too strong to say that forced ranking never does any good. In an organisation where years of inflated ratings have left no way of distinguishing good work from bad, a single round of hard comparison may expose problems that polite evaluation had concealed. The harm comes when a jolt is turned into a permanent regime, and the habits of comparison it encourages become the ordinary way in which colleagues regard one another.
R05-C-06: Inquiries into industrial disasters have a way of finding a culprit. An operator ignored a warning, an inspector signed a form he had not read, a manager overruled an engineer whose objections were inconvenient. Such findings are rarely false, but they are often beside the point, because they treat as a single failure of judgement what was in fact the end of a long and orderly process. Many organisations do not stumble into catastrophe; they walk towards it by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time. Consider a hypothetical chemical plant whose procedures say that a certain vessel must be shut down if its pressure exceeds a stated limit. One night the gauge registers a reading marginally above the permitted limit. Shutting down would be expensive, the excess is small, and the engineers on duty judge, correctly as it turns out, that the vessel is in no danger. Nothing untoward happens, and the next time the reading creeps over the limit there is a precedent, which makes the decision considerably easier. After a dozen such nights the limit has quietly moved: the written figure still stands in the manual, but the working figure, the one people actually act on, is higher. No one decided to change it. The change was made by the accumulated absence of harm. This is what makes the process so difficult to detect from within the organisation itself. Each step is defended by evidence, and the evidence is genuine, for the vessel really did not fail. What is mistaken is the inference drawn from it, that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small. Success becomes a reason for confidence, and confidence a reason to look less closely, so that the organisation's sense of its own safety grows at the same rate as its actual exposure to danger. By the time an outsider asks why the plant routinely runs above its limit, the question sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has. It does not follow that every departure from the rules is a step towards disaster. Written procedures are drafted in advance by people who cannot foresee every situation, and an organisation whose staff never deviated from them would be unable to adapt; much good practice begins as a sensible exception. The danger lies not in deviation itself but in deviation that is never recognised as such. A departure that is noticed, argued over and formally adopted is a decision; one that simply accumulates is drift, and drift answers to no one.
R05-C-07: Few words in the vocabulary of management carry as much reproach as slack. Idle machines, unfilled hours, inventory sitting in warehouses and staff whose days are not fully booked all appear, to the analyst armed with a spreadsheet, as resources that are paid for and not used. The programmes that set out to remove them, under whatever name is fashionable at the time, can usually point to impressive savings in their first year, and the savings are real. What such programmes measure less well is what the slack had been doing before it was removed, because its work was done in circumstances that the measurements were not designed to capture. The first of those circumstances is the shock. A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely, because there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor. A hospital ward staffed exactly to its average occupancy works smoothly in most weeks and is overwhelmed in the week that an infection spreads. In each case the margin that looked like waste was a store of capacity held against an event whose timing could not be known, and its value appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception. To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain. The second circumstance is less dramatic and perhaps more important. Organisations do not only respond to events; they also change themselves, and change requires time that is not already claimed. An engineer who has an afternoon free may try out an idea that no plan had scheduled; a manager with some unallocated budget can fund a small experiment without first writing a case for it that no one yet knows how to write. Most of these experiments come to nothing, which is exactly why a system that requires every hour and every rupee to be justified in advance will not permit them. The new products and methods that later look inevitable often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed. It would be naive to conclude that slack is always benign. Spare resources can shelter inefficiency as easily as invention, and a department with more staff than it needs may use the surplus not to experiment but to protect its own comfort or to fight for its standing within the firm. Some slack is indeed waste, and some of the people who defend it are defending their privileges. The critics of slack are therefore not simply wrong; they are answering a question that is badly posed. Asking how much slack an organisation has, and how quickly it can be reduced, treats a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform. The more useful question is what the slack is for and who can see it. A reserve whose purpose is understood, whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported can be defended on the days when it seems idle, and trimmed when it has outlived its purpose. A reserve that exists only because no one has looked at it will be either preserved for the wrong reasons or eliminated by the first auditor who does. The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it, but to hold it deliberately, as an organisation holds any other asset whose returns arrive irregularly.
R05-C-08: A durable genre of business writing proceeds by a method that looks, at first sight, impeccably empirical. The author selects a number of companies that have performed outstandingly over a long period, studies them closely, and identifies the practices they share: a strong culture, perhaps, or a fierce attention to customers, or a willingness to abandon unprofitable lines. These practices are then offered as the causes of greatness, and the reader who adopts them is invited to expect something of the same result. The books sell well, partly because the companies are vivid and partly because the method appears to replace opinion with evidence. The first difficulty is one of selection. By studying only the companies that succeeded, the method has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed. If a great many firms had strong cultures and attended closely to their customers, and most of them disappeared, then these traits are not what separated the winners from the rest; they were simply common, and the winners, being a subset of the many, happened to possess them as well. The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews. A second difficulty is subtler. Many of the traits that the method identifies are not observed independently of performance but described after the fact, by people who already know the result. A company that is doing well is said to have a bold strategy and a confident leadership; the same company, a few years later and in decline, is said to have been reckless and arrogant, though nothing in its conduct may have changed. The observers are not being dishonest when they do this; they are reading the same conduct in the light of what it later led to. Where descriptions of this kind are the raw material, the correlation between good practices and good results is partly manufactured by the way in which the practices were recognised. Defenders of the genre have an answer to the first point: compare the successful firms with a matched set of less successful ones, drawn from the same industries and periods. This is a real improvement and should be acknowledged as such. But it does not remove the second difficulty, since the comparison firms are still described by people who know how they fared, nor does it settle a third, which emerges only with time. Several of the companies held up as models in such studies later stumbled badly, and the explanation usually offered is that they abandoned the principles that had made them great. That explanation can be given whatever happens. A theory that accounts for success by the presence of certain practices, and for failure by their supposed absence, has arranged never to be wrong. None of this shows that the study of successful firms is worthless. Close accounts of how particular companies work can suggest hypotheses worth testing, and some of the practices they describe may well be beneficial. What the genre cannot do is what it most often claims to do: to identify, from the records of the winners, the reasons they won. A reader who wishes to learn from such books would do better to treat their lists of principles as questions rather than answers, and to remember that in a competitive market a large part of any outcome may be owed to timing and circumstance, which no one can copy.
